content.title: SIGNS YOU'RE ACTUALLY {{HEALTHIER}} THAN YOU THINK
facts: **Loud stomach growling** -> your migrating motor complex is sweeping leftover food debris through your gut between meals
**Sneezing in bright light** -> your optic nerve is wired tightly to your trigeminal nerve, a harmless crossed-wire reflex called photic sneezing
**Waking up starving** -> your metabolism ran efficiently overnight and your blood sugar dropped to a healthy baseline
**Sweating fast during exercise** -> your body has trained itself to cool down quicker, a sign of real cardiovascular fitness
**Yawning when someone else does** -> your brain's mirror neurons are functioning well, a marker of social and emotional connection
**Getting thirsty mid-workout** -> your hypothalamus is tracking hydration levels precisely instead of ignoring them
**Vivid, strange dreams** -> you're getting enough REM sleep, the stage tied to memory consolidation and mood regulation
**Cracking joints with no pain** -> gas bubbles releasing from joint fluid, not a sign of wear or damage
**Getting cold easily after eating light** -> your body is redirecting blood flow efficiently to digest what you just ate
**Random deep sighs throughout the day** -> your lungs resetting collapsed air sacs, a built-in breathing maintenance reflex

content.caption:
A few of these deserve a closer look. That loud **stomach growling** you get between meals isn't hunger complaining, it's your migrating motor complex, a wave of muscle contractions that sweeps leftover particles and bacteria through your intestines to keep things from building up. Waking up genuinely **starving** is another good sign, it usually means your liver did its job overnight, using stored glycogen to keep your blood sugar steady until morning instead of spiking and crashing. And those **vivid dreams** you sometimes remember in detail are a marker of solid REM sleep, the stage where your brain files away memories and processes emotions from the day. Of course, everyone's body runs a little differently, so use these as general signals, not diagnoses.
